title: Learning 𝜔-Powered Conditional Distributions with Importance-Weighted Flow Matching

paper.title: Learning ω \omega -Powered Conditional Distributions with Importance-Weighted Flow Matching
paper.abstract: Abstract Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) with guidance scale γ \gamma is commonly motivated by the ω \omega -powered conditional distribution obtained by setting ω = γ \omega=\gamma , but CFG does not, in general, sample from this distribution exactly. We study whether the powered target can instead be learned explicitly. We introduce Importance-Weighted Conditional Flow Matching (IW-CFM), which reweights conditional flow-matching examples using density ratios obtained from frozen conditional and unconditional flow models. With exact normalized weights, the resulting objective has the same gradient as flow matching on the powered target; in practice, we use self-normalized estimation and a regularized empirical approximation for high-dimensional data. On synthetic distributions, IW-CFM recovers analytical powered targets for which numerically matched CFG, γ = ω \gamma=\omega , exhibits a visible mismatch. On ImageNet, an amortized lightweight corrector achieves better alignment than fixed- and matched-guidance CFG with the corresponding weighted and filtered reference distributions. We additionally present an exploratory CLIP analysis of powered-density rankings on real ImageNet data. Aggregate shifts across selected prompt-specific contrasts coexist with heterogeneous classwise responses, including nonmonotonic trajectories. These results provide a practical route for studying and approximating model-defined powered conditional distributions. 1 1 1 Code and precomputed ImageNet log-probabilities are publicly available at https://bitbucket.org/dmmlgeneva/iw-cfm .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , flow matching (FM) ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , and stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) are widely used for continuous data such as images and audio. These methods learn a process between a simple prior, such as a Gaussian, and the data distribution. We work in the Gaussian flow-matching setting. Conditional models commonly use Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Dao et al., 2023 ) , which steers generation toward a condition y y by combining conditional and unconditional vector-field estimates. Both CFG and its predecessor, classifier-based guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , are motivated by a powered distribution , p ω ​ ( x | y ) ∝ p ​ ( x | y ) ω ​ p ​ ( x ) 1 − ω , p_{\omega}(x|y)\propto p(x|y)^{\omega}p(x)^{1-\omega}, (1) where ω > 1 \omega>1 is the powering parameter . Separately, we denote the CFG guidance scale by γ \gamma : CFG combines the conditional and unconditional vector fields as v CFG γ = γ v ( ⋅ | y ) + ( 1 − γ ) v ( ⋅ ) v_{\mathrm{CFG}}^{\gamma}=\gamma v(\cdot|y)+(1-\gamma)v(\cdot) . Its standard motivating interpretation identifies the two numerical values, γ = ω \gamma=\omega , and treats v CFG γ v_{\mathrm{CFG}}^{\gamma} as if it generated p ω p_{\omega} . This identification is not generally exact ( Bradley and Nakkiran, 2024 ; Chidambaram et al., 2024 ) : the CFG-guided backward vector field lacks a corresponding path-consistent forward process, and its endpoint distribution need not equal p ω p_{\omega} , even when γ = ω \gamma=\omega . The resulting mismatch can push probability mass away from the learned data manifold, manifesting as artifacts and unnatural saturation at high guidance scales. A related discrepancy has been identified in discrete diffusion models ( Kit et al., 2025 ) . We address the powered target directly by specializing conditional Energy-Weighted Flow Matching ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Density estimates from the conditional and unconditional flow models define the endpoint density ratio, and exact normalized weights yield the same population gradient as flow matching on the powered target. We call the resulting method Importance-Weighted Conditional Flow Matching (IW-CFM) ; it conditions on ω \omega and learns the flow for p ω ​ ( x | y ) p_{\omega}(x|y) without direct samples from that distribution. Any CFG subsequently applied to the learned IW-CFM vector field is an optional inference-time heuristic controlled separately by γ \gamma . Beyond target recovery, we examine how powered-density rankings of real images change with ω \omega . Using CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , which prior work has applied to image quality assessment ( Hentschel et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , we characterize selected prompt-specific contrasts and their classwise trajectories. Our main contributions are: • Building on Energy-Weighted Flow Matching ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , we instantiate endpoint weighting for model-defined ω \omega -powered conditional targets using density ratios from frozen conditional and unconditional flow models. • We develop a hierarchical self-normalized estimator for heterogeneous ( y , ω ) (y,\omega) pairs and distinguish this finite-sample procedure from the exact population objective. • We develop a lightweight corrector amortized over ω \omega and a high-dimensional ImageNet construction based on regularized precomputed weights, proposal sampling, and interpolation across powering parameters. • We validate recovery of analytical powered targets on synthetic distributions and measure alignment with regularized empirical references on ImageNet, where IW-CFM yields lower distances than the evaluated CFG baselines. • We provide an exploratory characterization of powered-density rankings on real images through selected CLIP contrasts, including heterogeneous and nonmonotonic classwise responses.

sections.heading: 2.5 Amortized ω \omega -Powering via Lightweight Correctors
sections.text: To avoid training a separate model for each powering parameter, we treat ω \omega as a conditioning variable for a single corrector network. We implement this corrector, v ϕ v^{\phi} , using lightweight, parameter-efficient designs. For synthetic experiments, v ϕ v^{\phi} is an MLP that predicts an affine correction to the baseline conditional vector field. For real-world image data (ImageNet), we build upon the Scalable Interpolant Transformer (SiT) backbone ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , introducing a parameter-efficient adapter into its Transformer blocks, similar to Jensen and Sadat (2025) . This way, we learn a single model to target the entire family of powered distributions, adding only about 5% of the parameters compared to the baseline SiT. A key challenge in this amortized setting is normalizing the importance weights. Normalizing globally across a batch with different conditions and powering parameters changes the effective distribution over ( y , ω ) (y,\omega) : each pair is weighted in proportion to its partition function Z ⁡ ( y , ω ) Z(y,\omega) rather than according to the intended outer distribution p ⁡ ( y ) ​ p ​ ( ω ) p(y)p(\omega) (see Section A.2 ). We instead use hierarchical batches and nested normalization. At each training step, we sample M M condition–parameter pairs ( y j , ω j ) (y_{j},\omega_{j}) and a subbatch of K K data points for each pair. We normalize weights only within samples that share ( y j , ω j ) (y_{j},\omega_{j}) , preserving the intended outer distribution. Algorithm 1 gives the procedure.

sections.heading: 2.6 Scaling to High-Dimensional Data
sections.text: Algorithm 1 provides an asymptotically unbiased estimator for streaming data, which we apply directly in our synthetic experiments. However, this approach is computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional data. We therefore adopt two practical techniques that enable an efficient application of IW-CFM to ImageNet. Amortized Training with Precomputed Weights. Sampling from the weighted empirical distribution at an arbitrary continuous ω \omega would require computing the weight of every ImageNet training instance for every sampled ω \omega . We instead precompute normalized weights over the full dataset at integer powering parameters. Given a continuous ω \omega , we sample training instances with replacement using the weights at the nearest integer m ¯ ​ ( ω ) \bar{m}(\omega) . For those instances only, we linearly interpolate the self-normalized weights at ω \omega and multiply the flow-matching loss by r ω reg ​ ( i | y ) / r m ¯ ​ ( ω ) reg ​ ( i | y ) r_{\omega}^{\mathrm{reg}}(i|y)/r_{\bar{m}(\omega)}^{\mathrm{reg}}(i|y) . This proposal is more efficient than uniform sampling followed by SNIS: at large ω \omega , most stored weights are zero, so most uniformly sampled instances would provide no weighted training signal. Section C.5.1 specifies the zero-weight fallback and numerical threshold. Operational ImageNet Weights. The population formulation assumes access to exact conditional and unconditional densities. On ImageNet, we instead use densities induced by frozen pretrained SiT vector fields, which are learned approximations to the data distributions, and evaluate them numerically through augmented ODE integration. Given any fixed set of endpoint weights, importance-weighted flow matching trains toward the distribution encoded by those weights. It does not, however, correct errors in the weights themselves. sections.heading: 3 Related Work
sections.text: The closest methodological predecessor is Energy-Weighted Flow Matching ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . At the population level, the IW-CFM objective is a specialization of their conditional energy-weighted flow-matching formulation. For a fixed condition y y , setting the base distribution to p ⁡ ( x | y ) p(x|y) , the energy to E y ​ ( x ) = log ⁡ p ⁡ ( x ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( x | y ) E_{y}(x)=\log p(x)-\log p(x|y) , and β = ω − 1 \beta=\omega-1 gives p ⁡ ( x | y ) ​ exp ⁡ [ − β ​ E y ​ ( x ) ] ∝ p ​ ( x | y ) ω ​ p ​ ( x ) 1 − ω . p(x|y)\exp[-\beta E_{y}(x)]\propto p(x|y)^{\omega}p(x)^{1-\omega}. Thus, the endpoint importance-weighting principle and the resulting population equivalence to flow matching on the reweighted target follow from Zhang et al. (2025) . Our contribution concerns the conditional, amortized, and high-dimensional realization of this principle. While Zhang et al. (2025) primarily develop energy-weighted generative models for offline reinforcement learning and additionally show, in a low-dimensional synthetic bandit ablation, that a single energy-weighted diffusion score model can be conditioned on β \beta , IW-CFM uses a lightweight flow-matching corrector to approximate model-defined powered conditional distributions across ImageNet classes and a continuous range of ω \omega . Our parameter-efficient corrector conditioned on ω \omega is inspired by guidance-distillation architectures ( Meng et al., 2023 ; Jensen and Sadat, 2025 ) , but is trained to approximate a family of powered vector fields rather than to reproduce standard CFG. This setting requires normalization across heterogeneous ( y , ω ) (y,\omega) pairs: our hierarchical estimator normalizes within each pair, preserving the intended outer distribution p ⁡ ( y ) ​ p ​ ( ω ) p(y)p(\omega) rather than reweighting pairs according to their partition functions. We further develop a regularized ImageNet construction based on precomputed conditional and unconditional densities, per-class weight regularization, nearest-integer proposal sampling, and interpolation between precomputed powering parameters. Our experiments evaluate recovery across a family of analytical synthetic targets and alignment with regularized ImageNet references. Analyses by Bradley and Nakkiran (2024) and Chidambaram et al. (2024) provide evidence that CFG does not generally sample from the powered distribution suggested by the numerical identification γ = ω \gamma=\omega and can shift probability mass away from the data manifold. These works diagnose the discrepancy; IW-CFM instead learns a vector field conditioned directly on the powering parameter ω \omega under the idealized formulation and its regularized empirical counterpart on ImageNet. Feynman–Kac Correctors (FKC) ( Skreta et al., 2025a ) use particle-based Sequential Monte Carlo to target modified distributions at inference time. Rectified Gradient Guidance (REG) ( Gao et al., 2025b ) formulates powered-distribution sampling as reward optimization over the sampling trajectory, while Kit et al. (2025) study a related debiasing problem for discrete diffusion. IW-CFM instead shifts the main computation to density precomputation and corrector training, after which sampling uses a single learned vector field. CFG++ ( Chung et al., 2025 ) modifies guidance to reduce off-manifold behavior, while Galashov et al. (2025) learn a guidance network that better matches the original conditional distribution p ⁡ ( x | y ) p(x|y) . Their target differs from ours: IW-CFM studies powered conditional distributions and a regularized empirical implementation on ImageNet. Finally, Karczewski et al. (2025) investigate extreme high-density regions of diffusion models and find that samples with substantially higher likelihood than those produced by standard samplers can be blank, blurry, or cartoon-like. Their results reinforce the distinction between model likelihood and perceptual quality. Our target differs from maximizing either the marginal or conditional likelihood in isolation: p ω ​ ( x | y ) p_{\omega}(x|y) increasingly emphasizes features discriminative of the condition. Their observations nevertheless motivate regularizing the concentrated importance weights in our ImageNet implementation.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our primary experiments address two questions. First, when the analytical ω \omega -powered density is available, does IW-CFM recover that target more faithfully than CFG with the numerically matched guidance scale γ = ω \gamma=\omega and the other evaluated alternatives? Second, on ImageNet, how closely do samples from the learned corrector align with weighted and filtered references derived from r ω reg r_{\omega}^{\mathrm{reg}} ? We study the first question on two-dimensional synthetic distributions and the second with a lightweight corrector for a pretrained SiT model. The exploratory analysis of powered-density rankings on real ImageNet data follows in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Synthetic Target Recovery
sections.text: We first test IW-CFM against the target density on two-dimensional synthetic datasets: a three-mode Gaussian mixture and a distribution inspired by fractal-like geometries (for details see Section C.1 ). For these tasks, we compute importance weights during training using the minibatch SNIS estimator in Algorithm 1 . As shown in Figures 1(a) and 1(b) , CFG with matched guidance γ = ω \gamma=\omega departs from the analytical target contours, whereas IW-CFM closely follows them. This controlled setting tests the motivating identification in Equation 5 before the density-estimation and regularization choices needed for ImageNet are introduced. Sections C.1 and D.3.1 provide hyperparameters and additional density visualizations. We additionally evaluate REG and FKC on the exact conditional and unconditional vector fields of the three-Gaussian problem. Under the tested configurations, neither method closely matches the analytical powered contours. We therefore do not conduct an image-scale comparison, and our ImageNet results make no claim of superiority over REG or FKC. Section D.3.2 provides implementation details and results.

sections.heading: 4.2 ImageNet Generation
sections.text: We scale our method to ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. The IW-CFM corrector operates in the latent space of the Stable Diffusion VAE used by the pretrained SiT model ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Log-probability computation, loss reweighting, and sampling all use this latent space; we decode to pixels only for visualization and image-based metrics (CLIP, FID, and DINOv2). The corrector is a parameter-efficient adapter in the frozen Transformer blocks of a pretrained SiT-XL/2 ( Ma and Ryoo, 2024 ) , following Jensen and Sadat (2025) . sections.heading: 4.4 Ablation of the ImageNet Experiment
sections.text: We independently ablate two components of the ImageNet implementation: the numerical accuracy of log-density estimation and the regularization applied to the resulting importance weights. In each experiment, all other settings are held fixed. Number of log-density integration steps. We conduct this ablation on a fixed subset of 100 ImageNet categories, described in Section C.6.1 , while keeping the target-regularization parameters at their default values. For each evaluated step count, we recompute the log-densities and importance weights and train a new corrector from scratch. All models are evaluated against the common weighted and filtered references constructed from the 250-step log-density estimates, using 50 generated samples per category. As shown in Figure 3 , the results remain relatively close at ω ∈ { 4 , 8 } \omega\in\{4,8\} , begin to separate at ω = 16 \omega=16 , and diverge substantially for ω ≥ 32 \omega\geq 32 . This behavior is consistent with the error-amplification effect discussed in Section 2.6 : an additive error in the estimated log-density ratio is multiplied by ω − 1 \omega-1 before exponentiation. Consequently, the numerical precision used for density estimation should be selected according to the largest powering parameter of interest; a step count adequate at small ω \omega need not remain adequate under stronger powering. sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: IW-CFM has several limitations. First, it depends on the quality and support coverage of the base density models. The ImageNet implementation also depends on regularized precomputed weights, nearest-integer sampling, and interpolation. Computing these weights requires a correction dataset. We use that dataset to correct a pretrained model rather than train one from scratch, but performance may change when the correction data are smaller than or shifted from the original training set. Second, density precomputation requires solving two augmented ODEs, one conditional and one unconditional, for each training instance. This one-time cost enables sampling with a single learned corrector. The ImageNet weight construction has a separate regularization trade-off : log-weight clipping and temperature scaling limit concentration on a few training modes, but their settings are chosen manually. Automated regularization schedules remain future work. Our CLIP analysis is descriptive and prompt-dependent; consequently, neither the class-averaged trajectories nor individual examples establish statistically significant or universal attribute effects. Finally, our current nested estimator and ImageNet implementation are tailored to categorical conditioning because self-normalization groups samples by a shared class label. The population formulation itself does not require categorical conditions. Applying the practical estimator to high-cardinality or continuous conditions, such as text prompts, will require a different normalization strategy.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusions
sections.text: In this work, we introduced Importance-Weighted Conditional Flow Matching (IW-CFM) to learn model-defined ω \omega -powered conditional distributions. With exact densities and normalization, its population objective targets the powered vector field. The practical finite-sample estimator uses self-normalized weights, and the ImageNet implementation uses regularized precomputed integer weights with interpolated per-sample corrections. The synthetic experiments test the analytical target directly and show that IW-CFM recovers it more faithfully than the evaluated alternatives, including CFG at the numerically matched scale γ = ω \gamma=\omega . On ImageNet, the learned corrector aligns more closely than CFG with the weighted and filtered regularized references. Unguided evaluation provides evidence of a learned distributional shift, while the guided practical results include an additional inference-time CFG heuristic and therefore do not isolate the distributional shift learned by the corrector. The complementary real-image analysis shows that powered-density rankings and their selected CLIP contrasts vary with ω \omega . The across-class averages exhibit several baseline-relative shifts, while the underlying classwise trajectories are heterogeneous and can be decreasing or nonmonotonic. IW-CFM learns multiple powered targets with one corrector. Although our implementation uses a SiT backbone, the population formulation applies to other continuous domains. Applying it to video or 3D synthesis would require testing the available density estimates, normalization schemes, and operational targets in those settings.

sections.heading: Broader Impact Statement
sections.text: This work studies generative modeling of images, with the technical goal of producing realistic and diverse samples. That goal is not socially neutral: greater realism makes synthetic images harder to distinguish from photographic evidence, while greater diversity broadens the range of content that can be generated at scale. These capabilities may support valuable scientific and creative applications, but they may also facilitate deception, impersonation, non-consensual imagery, and other forms of abuse. Improvements in generative modeling should therefore be accompanied by careful evaluation of misuse risks and appropriate safeguards in any deployed system.

sections.text: Nested normalization uses M M condition–parameter pairs ( y , ω ) (y,\omega) , each with a subbatch of K K data samples and finite-batch weights w ^ ω , K \widehat{w}_{\omega,K} . Under standard finite-variance assumptions, the leading variance terms scale as 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / M ) \mathcal{O}(1/M) across ( y , ω ) (y,\omega) pairs and 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / ( M ​ K ) ) \mathcal{O}(1/(MK)) for within-pair Monte Carlo noise. With fixed B = M ​ K B=MK , these terms become 𝒪 ⁡ ( K / B ) \mathcal{O}(K/B) and 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / B ) \mathcal{O}(1/B) , respectively. Increasing K K reduces finite- K K SNIS bias but leaves fewer distinct ( y , ω ) (y,\omega) pairs for estimating the outer expectation. sections.heading: C.3 Base Model Density Computational Cost
sections.text: For the main results presented in the paper the augmented ODE for log-probability evaluation ( Equation 6 ) uses a first-order Euler solver with 250 steps. sections.heading: C.5 SiT Corrector: Implementation and Training Details
sections.text: To scale our method to ImageNet, we implement the IW-CFM corrector as a parameter-efficient adapter integrated into a frozen SiT-XL/2 backbone. The architecture and parameter-efficient conditioning follow the design of Jensen and Sadat (2025) . Training Strategy and Efficiency. We precompute the normalized importance weights on an integer grid. For each continuous ω ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 4,128 ] \omega\sim\mathcal{U}[4,128] , the ImageNet data loader rounds to the nearest grid point m ¯ ​ ( ω ) \bar{m}(\omega) and samples examples with replacement according to the stored sampling weights at that point. For each sampled instance i i , we interpolate the unmodified weights at the adjacent grid points to obtain r ω reg ​ ( i | y ) r_{\omega}^{\mathrm{reg}}(i|y) . The flow-matching loss is multiplied by r ω reg ​ ( i | y ) / r m ¯ ​ ( ω ) reg ​ ( i | y ) r_{\omega}^{\mathrm{reg}}(i|y)/r_{\bar{m}(\omega)}^{\mathrm{reg}}(i|y) when the denominator exceeds 10 − 9 10^{-9} , and by one otherwise. The unit fallback gives re-injected training examples an unweighted flow-matching loss; these examples would otherwise receive zero weight. It also avoids division by a numerically zero stored weight. We therefore interpolate weights only for sampled instances. This avoids the nested normalization in Algorithm 1 during corrector training and is more efficient than uniform sampling followed by self-normalized weighting, for which most sampled examples would have zero loss weight. • We train with a global batch size of 256 distributed across 8 GPUs. • Normalizing independently on each GPU’s local subbatch would reduce the normalization-group size, lowering the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing variance. • The precomputed proposal and correction weights are shared across workers. Optimizer and Schedule. We use Adam with β 1 = 0.5 \beta_{1}=0.5 , β 2 = 0.9 \beta_{2}=0.9 , and a base learning rate of 1.0 × 10 − 3 1.0\times 10^{-3} . We train for 45,000 iterations with a 2,000-iteration linear warmup followed by cosine decay. Evaluation Setup. We sample with a Heun solver using 250 function evaluations (125 steps). At each ω \omega , we generate 50,000 instances (50 per ImageNet class). The computational cost of training the corrector is approximately 96 GPUhours on a RTX A6000. In Table 3 we report the overhead of the corrector during inference on a RTX 4090. For each of the setups we run 10 independent measurements, each preceded by proper warming up. We report the comparison on a single forward run, on the full sampling with a 250-NFE Heun sampler, as well as, sampling with decoding to image space. All experiments are run in both batch size 1 and 24 setups, in eager and compiled mode. While the overhead in batch size 1 eager mode is noticeable (more than 20%) the difference is decreasing significantly (to less than 1% in certain setups) with batch size 24 and/or compiled mode. sections.text: To assess whether IW-CFM retrieves high-likelihood training instances rather than generating novel variations, we conduct a nearest-neighbor analysis. This test asks whether training-data retrieval could explain the observed distribution-alignment and paired-CLIP score differences. Methodology. We follow the framework of Gu et al. (2025) . After deduplicating the training set as described below, we flatten the VAE latent tensors and compute Euclidean distances from each generated sample to every remaining training instance. We apply no additional distance filter before sorting these distances. Let d 1 ≤ d 2 d_{1}\leq d_{2} be the two smallest distances. This setting requires normalization across heterogeneous ( y , ω ) (y,\omega) pairs: our hierarchical estimator normalizes within each pair, preserving the intended outer distribution p ⁡ ( y ) ​ p ​ ( ω ) p(y)p(\omega) rather than reweighting pairs according to their partition functions. We further develop a regularized ImageNet construction based on precomputed conditional and unconditional densities, per-class weight regularization, nearest-integer proposal sampling, and interpolation between precomputed powering parameters. Our experiments evaluate recovery across a family of analytical synthetic targets and alignment with regularized ImageNet references. Analyses by Bradley and Nakkiran (2024) and Chidambaram et al. (2024) provide evidence that CFG does not generally sample from the powered distribution suggested by the numerical identification γ = ω \gamma=\omega and can shift probability mass away from the data manifold. These works diagnose the discrepancy; IW-CFM instead learns a vector field conditioned directly on the powering parameter ω \omega under the idealized formulation and its regularized empirical counterpart on ImageNet.
